sections.title: Is it normal to want to stay in shutdown even when I know safety would be better?
Why can't I climb my polyvagal ladder even when I'm trying all the "right" techniques?
How long should I stay in a defensive state before trying to move up the ladder?
What if accepting my defensive state makes me feel lazy or weak?
Can I be in a defensive state and still function in daily life?
When should I seek professional help for "polyvagal resistance"?

blocks.p: Have you ever noticed that even when you know being in your [safety state](hub:safety) would feel better, part of you wants to stay stuck in shutdown or fight-or-flight? You're not alone! (And you're definitely not broken.)

Do you find yourself resisting the very thing you learn about that could help you recover? Maybe you've learned about the [polyvagal theory and understand the three nervous system states](piece:snb101-polyvagal-101-foundations), but when it comes to actually climbing your polyvagal ladder to safety, your body seems to fight back.

If this sounds familiar, you're experiencing what I'll call "polyvagal resistance," and it's far more common than you might think. As a therapist, I regularly hear from clients who struggle with this exact issue.
The good news? This "Polyvagal resistance" isn't a character flaw or a sign that you're "doing it wrong." It's actually your nervous system trying to communicate something important to you.

blocks.h: Understanding Polyvagal resistance: you're not broken

blocks.p: Let's start with a fundamental truth: your defensive states exist for a reason. Whether fight-or-flight or shutdown, these states evolved within us to help us survive. They're not inherently "good" or "bad." They simply are.
Even if you have a stuck defensive state, it's still not good or bad, even if it feels that way. A stuck state indicates there is an underlying impulse that needs to be acted upon.

When you experience resistance to climbing your polyvagal ladder, it often means there's an impulse from your defensive state that hasn't been met yet. Think of it like your nervous system saying, "Hold on, I'm not done here yet. There's something I need to complete first."

For example, you may learn that extending your exhale helps you access safety. But if you're in flight/fight, extending your exhale is a challenge. The flight/fight state is not prepared to execute a behavior that could help you access safety.
And then you're left wondering, "Why am I resistant?"

Or, you may have learned that taking daily walks can help relieve your shutdown. Great, now you just need to go for a walk every day, right? Yes, but… shutdown doesn't like movement! So, your [shutdown state](hub:shutdown) is not mobilized enough to walk every day.
And then you're left wondering, "Why am I resistant?"
This resistance becomes even more understandable when you consider that your polyvagal state is highly context-dependent. Your nervous system is constantly responding to:

ul: Your immediate environment (sounds, lighting, space)
The people around you and their nervous system states
Larger life circumstances and stressors
Past experiences and trauma patterns

blocks.p: For example, I notice that when my heater runs, it creates a low background hum that activates a subtle fight-or-flight response in my system. When it turns off, I can feel my nervous system settle. These seemingly minor environmental factors significantly impact our capacity to access our safety state.

blocks.h: Why your nervous system fights safety (3 common reasons)

blocks.h3: 1. Unfinished business: when your body has unmet impulses

blocks.p: Your resistance might indicate that your body has specific impulses it needs to complete before it can safely move up the polyvagal ladder.
Shutdown impulses can include:

ul: reduced sensory stimulation
collapse
solitude

blocks.p: Flight/fight impulses can include:

ul: squeezing, pushing, pulling
sprinting, walking, jogging

blocks.p: These aren't character flaws, they're biological needs. Fighting against them keeps you stuck longer than honoring them would.

blocks.h3: 2. Environmental challenges to your safety state

blocks.p: Your nervous system is constantly scanning for safety and danger cues, many of which operate below your conscious awareness. Consider how these factors might be challenging your access to safety:

ul: Physical environment: Noise, lighting, crowding, temperature
Social environment: Being around people stuck in their own defensive states
Cultural and family factors: Larger societal stressors and expectations
Life circumstances: Financial stress, relationship challenges, health concerns

blocks.p: Even positive changes can challenge your safety state. Getting married, having children, starting a new job, or other growth experiences naturally activate defensive states because they're new and unfamiliar.

blocks.h3: 3. Life transitions naturally challenge your nervous system

blocks.p: Here's something most people don't realize: challenging your safety state capacity throughout life is actually healthy and necessary for growth.
I don't think we should wait until everything feels perfectly comfortable before taking our next steps. The fact that something feels challenging often means you're on the right path for growth.
The key is learning to stay anchored in safety while experiencing defensive activation, rather than trying to eliminate the defensive response entirely.

blocks.h: The truth about "wanting" to stay in defense

blocks.p: I received an email from a fellow therapist, whom I'll call "Diana." She wrote:

q: I noticed lots of resistance to moving up my polyvagal ladder. I was recognizing in myself a desire to stay in that shutdown space. When I'm not in shutdown, I can see the benefit of moving into safety, but when I am shut down, I kind of want to be left alone to just stay in my misery.

blocks.p: If you can relate to Diana's experience, you're not alone. But let's reframe what's happening here. And instead of focusing on shutdown, I'll address it generally from defense.
Instead of "I want to stay in defense," try "My body needs something from this defensive state."
This shift moves you from judgment to curiosity, from fighting your state to working with it. When you're in defense, that "want" to stay there might actually be your body's way of saying:

ul: "I need time to process."
"I need to complete some biological impulse."
"I need space to be with what I'm experiencing."

blocks.prompt: When part of you wants to stay put, what might your body need from that state? Finish the sentence: "My body needs..."

blocks.p: The goal isn't to eliminate these needs, it's to honor them while staying anchored in enough safety to witness what's happening.

blocks.h: How to work with resistance (not against it)

blocks.p: The traditional approach to trauma recovery often focuses on "getting out of" defensive states. I believe this approach is not only ineffective but potentially disrespectful to your nervous system's wisdom.
Use this three-step practice proactively, meaning before the skill is needed. Don't wait for defensive activation to spike and then practice this. That would be reactive.

blocks.h3: Step 1: accept where you are (no fighting required)

blocks.p: Accepting your defensive state doesn't mean giving up or staying stuck forever. It means acknowledging what's true right now without judgment.
When you notice resistance to climbing your polyvagal ladder:

ul: Notice the resistance without trying to change it
Acknowledge the resistance through naming it
Normalize the resistance, and that defensive states serve important functions

blocks.h3: Step 2: anchor in safety while honoring your defensive state

blocks.p: This is the most important piece that most people, including professionals, miss: anchoring in safety doesn't mean eliminating defensive activation. It means staying regulated while experiencing whatever defensive energy is present.

In Step 2, you will do something to anchor into your safety state. There are numerous paths to anchoring into safety and concrete meditations to follow on the [Unstucking Pathway](https://www.stucknotbroken.com/checkout/co-regulator) inside of the Unstucking Academy.
When you successfully balance safety and defense, the defensive activation turns into something else:

ul: regulated fight energy feels like power and motivation rather than out-of-control aggression
regulated shutdown allows for rest and processing rather than complete collapse

blocks.why: Step 2 is anchoring in safety while you let the defensive state be there. This practice is that step, tuned to you.

blocks.p: For more detailed strategies on working specifically with shutdown states, see [Dorsal vagal shutdown: symptoms, how long it lasts, and the way out](piece:dorsal-vagal-shutdown).

blocks.h3: Step 3: listen to your body's impulses

blocks.p: Once you're anchored in safety while allowing your defensive state, you can begin to explore what your body actually needs.
From a balanced and curious place, ask yourself:

ul: What does my body need right now?
What impulses am I experiencing?
What would feel supportive in this moment?

blocks.p: For shutdown specifically, this might mean:

ul: Creating a lower-stimulation environment (dimmer lights, quieter space)
Allowing yourself to move more slowly
Honoring the need for solitude without judgment
Giving yourself permission to be immobile

blocks.p: The key is listening to these impulses without judgment, which requires being anchored in your safety state. These types of practices get far easier over time. Again, practice these proactively, before resistance increases to the point of dysregulation.

blocks.h: Practical steps to reduce Polyvagal resistance

blocks.p: Pay attention to how your environment affects your nervous system:

ul: Sound: Notice background noises that might activate fight-or-flight (fans, traffic, appliances)
Movement: If stuck in flight/fight, have fidgets or exercise bands ready to use
Stimulation levels: Reduce overwhelming sensory input when in shutdown

blocks.p: Practice observing your resistance from a curious, third-person perspective:

ol: Notice: "I'm experiencing resistance to moving up my polyvagal ladder."
Reframe: "My body has needs that haven't been met yet."
Explore: "What might my nervous system be trying to tell me?"
Honor: "How can I respect these needs while staying anchored in safety?"

blocks.p: Consider working with a polyvagal-informed therapist if:

ul: You feel stuck in defensive states for extended periods
Your resistance interferes significantly with daily functioning
You're struggling to access any degree of safety state
You need support navigating complex trauma responses

blocks.p: If stuck in shutdown, learn more about [understanding dorsal vagal shutdown](piece:dorsal-vagal-shutdown) and how it relates to resistance patterns.

blocks.h: Moving forward: building your capacity for growth

blocks.p: Remember that experiencing resistance to polyvagal ladder climbing is normal, though no, not ideal. It indicates that your nervous system is trying to communicate important information about your needs and capacity.
The goal isn't to eliminate resistance but to develop the skills to:

ul: Work with your resistance rather than against it
Stay anchored in safety while experiencing defensive activation
Listen to and honor your body's impulses
Gradually build your capacity to handle life's challenges while maintaining nervous system regulation

blocks.h3: Is it normal to want to stay in shutdown even when I know safety would be better?

blocks.p: Absolutely. What feels like "wanting" to stay in shutdown is often your body communicating unmet needs. Your nervous system isn't being stubborn, it's telling you there are impulses or processes that need completion before it feels safe to move up the polyvagal ladder.

blocks.h3: Why can't I climb my polyvagal ladder even when I'm trying all the "right" techniques?

blocks.p: Resistance often indicates your nervous system has unfinished business. Instead of trying harder to climb the ladder, accept where you are and listen to what your defensive state needs. Fighting your nervous system usually keeps you stuck longer than honoring its messages.

blocks.h3: How long should I stay in a defensive state before trying to move up the ladder?

blocks.p: There's no set timeline. Your nervous system will naturally want to move toward safety once its needs are met. Focus on anchoring in enough safety to observe your defensive state with curiosity rather than rushing to "fix" it.

blocks.h3: What if accepting my defensive state makes me feel lazy or weak?

blocks.p: These judgments often come from misunderstanding what acceptance means. Accepting your defensive state isn't giving up. It's the first step in working effectively with your nervous system. You can't regulate what you won't acknowledge.

blocks.h3: Can I be in a defensive state and still function in daily life?

blocks.p: Yes! The goal isn't to eliminate defensive states but to stay anchored enough in safety that you can function while experiencing them. This is what we call being "regulated" rather than "perfect."

blocks.h3: When should I seek professional help for "polyvagal resistance"?

blocks.p: Consider working with a polyvagal-informed therapist if you feel stuck in defensive states for extended periods, if resistance significantly interferes with daily life, or if you're struggling to access any degree of safety state on your own. (As a reminder, "polyvagal resistance" is not a term used outside of this article. It's not a diagnosis of any kind.)
